chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: [Enter the blind OEDIPUS, led by his daughter ANTIGONE.]

OEDIPUS. Antigone, child of an old blind father — tell me, what country is this? Whose city have we reached? Who today will offer even a meager handout to this wanderer? He asks for little, and gets less — but that little is enough for me. Suffering has taught me to endure, and so have the long years that have grown old alongside me, and not least my own true nobility. My daughter, if you see any resting place on common ground or beside some sacred grove, stop me and set me down. Let us find out where we have come; strangers must ask those who live here, and do whatever they are told.

ANTIGONE. My long-suffering father, Oedipus — the towers that guard the city are still faint and far away. But the ground where we stand is surely holy: a wilderness of laurel, olive, and vine, and inside it a chorus of nightingales is singing. Rest here on this native seat of rock; for an old man, you have traveled far.
OEDIPUS. Guide these blind steps, and sit me down there safely.
ANTIGONE. After all this time, you don't have to tell me.
OEDIPUS. Please, if you know — tell me where we are.
ANTIGONE. I recognize Athens, but not this particular place.
OEDIPUS. That much we heard from every traveler on the road.
ANTIGONE. Shall I go and ask someone about the place?
OEDIPUS. Yes, daughter, if the area is inhabited.
ANTIGONE. There are houses here, certainly — but I don't need to leave you. There is a man nearby.
OEDIPUS. What — moving toward us, already on his way?
ANTIGONE. Better to say he is already here. Ask him whatever you need to ask; the man is right here.
[Enter STRANGER.]
OEDIPUS. Stranger — I learn from her, whose eyes must serve both of us, that you have been sent here by some lucky chance to resolve our questions —
STRANGER. First, get up from that seat, and then ask me whatever you wish. The spot you are sitting on is holy ground.
OEDIPUS. What is this place? To what god is it dedicated?
STRANGER. No one may touch it or walk on it. Goddesses live here — the dreaded daughters of Earth and Darkness.
OEDIPUS. Tell me the awful name I should call them by.
STRANGER. Our people here call them the Gracious Ones, the All-seeing. Elsewhere they go by other names.
OEDIPUS. Then may they show gracious welcome to their suppliant — for I will never leave this sanctuary of yours.
STRANGER. What do you mean by that?
OEDIPUS. The password of my destiny.
STRANGER. It isn't for me to send you away without proper authority and instructions from the State.
OEDIPUS. For god's sake, stranger, don't dismiss me as some common wanderer. Tell me what I'm asking.
STRANGER. Ask. Your question won't be dismissed by me.
OEDIPUS. What do you call this place, where we are now?

STRANGER. Whatever I know, you will know. The whole place is consecrated to great Poseidon. Nearby, the Titan who carries the torch, Prometheus, is worshiped. But the exact spot you are standing on is called the Bronze-footed Threshold — the bulwark of Athens. And the neighboring lands claim as their chief and patron that knight Colonus over there, and all share his name. That, stranger, is what this place is: not famous to the world, but dear to us who were born here and worship here.
OEDIPUS. So there are people living in this area?
STRANGER. Of course. They carry the name of that god over there.
OEDIPUS. Are they ruled by a king, or by the common vote?
STRANGER. The lord of Athens is our overlord.
OEDIPUS. Who is this monarch, powerful in word and might?
STRANGER. Theseus, son of our late king Aegeus.
OEDIPUS. Could someone from here be sent to summon him?
STRANGER. Why? To give him some message, or to urge him to come?
OEDIPUS. Say that a small service on his part may bring him great gain.
STRANGER. What benefit can he get from a blind man?
OEDIPUS. The blind man's words will be full of sight.

STRANGER. Listen, then — I'd like to keep you out of trouble. By your looks, ruined though they are by fate, I judge you to be noble. Stay where you are while I go find the locals — the ones nearby, not in the city. They will decide soon enough whether you should stay or move on.
[Exit STRANGER.]
OEDIPUS. Tell me, daughter — has the stranger gone?
ANTIGONE. Yes, he's gone. We are completely alone now, and you can speak freely, dear father.

OEDIPUS. Stern-faced queens — since coming to this land I have bent my knee first at your sanctuary. Do not frown on me, or on Phoebus. When he long ago told me all the miseries still to come, he also spoke of this respite, after many years: a refuge in a far-off land, a rest granted at last by dread divinities. "There," he said, "you shall round off your weary life — a blessing to the land you settle in, and a curse to the land that cast you out." He promised signs would come to mark my fate: earthquake, or thunderclap, or flash of lightning. And now I recognize the sign as yours — the sign that guided my wanderings into this grove of yours. Otherwise I would never have come upon you first, a man without wine for an offering, resting on your native rock. Goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word. Grant me some final resolution of my life, if I do not seem altogether vile, a slave to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear me, gentle daughters of primeval Night. Hear, city that bears the name of great Pallas — Athens, first of cities, pity this dishonored shade, the ghost of the man who once was Oedipus.
ANTIGONE. Hush! I see some old men on their way, coming to find out who is resting here.
OEDIPUS. I will say nothing. Guide my steps off the public road into the cover of the grove, until I have learned what they intend. A prudent man always shapes his course by what he learns.

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: [Enter CHORUS.]

CHORUS. Look! Where is he? Look around! Search every corner, every nook! That all-presuming man — where has he gone? Search the ground! A traveler, I'd say, a traveler and no native of ours — that old man must have been. Never would one of our people dare to provoke the Powers, or set foot in their sanctuary — the Maidens before whom every mortal trembles, whose name no voice utters, no cry names. When we pass them, we look away, and move our lips in hushed, reverent prayer. But now some godless man, it's said, is hiding here. I scan the whole precinct, and still can't find where he is hiding — the reckless wretch! I search and search in vain.
OEDIPUS. I am that man. I know you are near — they say the ears of a blind man are his eyes.
CHORUS. Terrible to see, and terrible to hear!
OEDIPUS. Sirs, I am not an outlaw under sentence.
CHORUS. Who can he be — Zeus save us! — this old man?

OEDIPUS. Not a favorite of fortune — not so lucky that you should envy his condition. Sirs, would any happy mortal grope his way by the light of another's eyes, or lean on so frail a support against the storm?

CHORUS. Were you blind from birth, then? Your life on earth has been long, and full of evil, I'd say. Yet don't add curse to curse and wrong to wrong. I warn you: do not trespass on this hallowed ground. Stop before you reach the silent grassy glade where offerings are laid — bowls of spring water mixed with sweet mead. You must not stay. Come away, come away — weary wanderer, are you listening? (We are far off, but our voice surely carries to you.) If you want to make some plea, speak where it's allowed; until then, hold your tongue.
OEDIPUS. Daughter, what should we do now?
ANTIGONE. We must obey and do as they do here.
OEDIPUS. Your hand, then!
ANTIGONE. Here, father — here is my hand.
OEDIPUS. Sirs, if I come out at your command, do not let me suffer for trusting you.
CHORUS. No one will force you out against your will.
OEDIPUS. Shall I come further?
CHORUS. Yes.
OEDIPUS. Further still?
CHORUS. Lead him, girl — you can guide him where we want.
ANTIGONE. [Text lost in manuscript.]
OEDIPUS. [Text lost in manuscript.]
ANTIGONE. [Text lost in manuscript.]
Follow with your blind steps, father, as I lead you.
OEDIPUS. [Text lost in manuscript.]
CHORUS. You are a stranger in a strange land — bend your will to hers. Honor whatever the State honors, and hate what she frowns on.
OEDIPUS. Guide me, child, so we may move safely along the paths of what is right. Let us speak freely, and not fight against fate or fortune.
CHORUS. Halt! Go no further than that rocky floor.
OEDIPUS. Stay where I am now?
CHORUS. Yes, come no further.
OEDIPUS. May I sit down?
CHORUS. Move sideways to the ledge, and sit crouched on the cut edge.
ANTIGONE. That is my job, father — lean on me.
OEDIPUS. Oh, oh!
ANTIGONE. Match your steps to mine; rest your old frame against me.
OEDIPUS. Misery on my wretched fate!
CHORUS. Wanderer, now that you are at rest — tell me your birth and your home. From what far country have you come, led on this weary journey? Speak!
OEDIPUS. Strangers, I have no country. Do not press me —
CHORUS. What is it, old man, that you want to hide?
OEDIPUS. Stop — do not push me to reveal it —
CHORUS. Why this reluctance?
OEDIPUS. My birth is a thing of horror.
CHORUS. Speak!
OEDIPUS. What am I to say, child? Alas!
CHORUS. Tell us your lineage — whose son you are —
OEDIPUS. Oh, daughter — now we are ruined!
ANTIGONE. Speak — you stand on the slippery edge.
OEDIPUS. I will. There is no plea for silence I can make.
CHORUS. Why do neither of you speak? Come, sir, why this delay!
OEDIPUS. Do you know any son of Laius —
CHORUS. Ha! Who?
OEDIPUS. Of the line of Labdacus —
CHORUS. O Zeus!
OEDIPUS. The luckless Oedipus.
CHORUS. Is it you?
OEDIPUS. Whatever I say, do not be afraid of me.
CHORUS. Begone!
OEDIPUS. Oh, I am wretched!
CHORUS. Begone!
OEDIPUS. Daughter, what will happen now?
CHORUS. Out of our borders, both of you — quickly!
OEDIPUS. Then how do you keep your promise?

CHORUS. Heaven's justice never strikes the man who repays evil with evil. But if one guile contends with another guile, the end is ruin, not blessing. Get up, leave, go at once — so that you lay no heavier curse on our land.

ANTIGONE. Sirs! You would not have turned away my blind father if, though gracious and inclined to pity, you knew the deeds he committed — not innocent, but done with no evil intent. Still, listen to a girl's plea for him, a girl who pleads for him alone. My eyes are not robbed of sight. They plead with you as a daughter's eyes can. You are our only hope — do not drive us from here! With one gracious nod, grant us this mercy we had almost given up on. Hear us, hear us — by all that you hold dear: wife, children, home, hearth, and God! Search as hard as you like — where will you find a single man who escapes destruction if a god drives him on?
CHORUS. We pity you both alike, daughter of Oedipus, for your suffering. But because we honor the decrees of Heaven, we cannot say anything different from what we have said.

OEDIPUS. What is the use of a famous name and a good reputation? Isn't it all vanity? For look — Athens is said to be the most devout of all states. Athens alone, they say, gives hospitality and shelter to the harassed stranger. Have I found it so? No — I whom you first dislodged from my seat of rock, and now want to drive out of your land, afraid of my name alone. You surely aren't afraid of me myself, or of my deeds — the deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning, as I could easily prove to you, if it were right to tell the story of my mother and my father, the cause of this fear of yours. Am I then a villain by birth, because in self-defense, when struck, I struck the striker back? Even if I had known who he was, it would not have been villainy. But I went where I went without knowing anything — went to ruin — while those who destroyed me knew perfectly well. So I beg you, sirs, in Heaven's name: since you told me to leave my seat, now defend me. Do not pay lip service to the gods and cheat them of what is due to them. Think carefully: the eye of Heaven sees the just and the unjust alike, and never yet in this world has one single godless sinner escaped. Stand on Heaven's side, and do not blot the fair name of Athens by helping injustice. I came to you as a suppliant; you pledged your honor. Protect me to the end. Do not let this ruined face count against me. A holy, god-fearing man is here, and his coming brings comfort to your people. When your chief arrives, whoever he is, you shall hear my story and know everything. Meanwhile, I beg you: do me no wrong.
CHORUS. The case you make, weighty as it is, gives us pause — but we must leave the decision to those who rule.
OEDIPUS. Where is he, strangers — the man who rules this land?
CHORUS. In his ancestral seat. A messenger — the same man who sent us here — has gone to bring him.
OEDIPUS. And do you think he will care enough about a blind stranger to come himself?
CHORUS. Yes, he will, once he hears your name.
OEDIPUS. But who will bring him the message?

CHORUS. The road is long, and many travelers pass along it and will carry the news. Be sure he will hear and come quickly, have no fear. Your name is so widely known that, however tired or reluctant, he would rouse himself at once when he hears of you.
OEDIPUS. Well, may he come with blessing for his State and for me! Whoever serves his neighbor serves himself.
ANTIGONE. Zeus! What is this? What am I to say or think?
OEDIPUS. What is it now, Antigone?

ANTIGONE. I see a woman riding a colt of Aetna's breed. For a hat she wears a Thessalian sunshade to keep off the sun. Who can it be? Her — or a stranger? Am I awake or dreaming? It is her — it isn't — I can't tell, alas. It is no one else! Now her face brightens as she recognizes me — yes, it is her, herself, Ismene!
OEDIPUS. What! What are you saying, child?
ANTIGONE. I see your daughter and my sister — and you will know her at once by her voice.

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: [Enter ISMENE.]
ISMENE. Father and sister — names dearest in the world to me — how hard it was to find you, and now that I have found you at last, how hard even to see you through my tears!
OEDIPUS. You have come, my child?
ISMENE. O father, your situation is dreadful!
OEDIPUS. Child, you are here?
ISMENE. Yes — it was a weary road.
OEDIPUS. Touch me, my child.
ISMENE. I give a hand to each of you.
OEDIPUS. Oh, my children — my daughters!
ISMENE. What a disastrous state you are in!
OEDIPUS. My state, and hers?
ISMENE. Yes — and mine no less.
OEDIPUS. What brought you, daughter?
ISMENE. Father — concern for you.
OEDIPUS. A daughter's longing to see me?
ISMENE. Yes, and I had news I wanted to deliver myself — so I came, along with the one servant still loyal to me.
OEDIPUS. Your brave brothers — where are they, when you need them?
ISMENE. They are — well, this is their darkest hour.

OEDIPUS. Curse them both! Their thoughts and actions are all modeled on Egyptian customs. In Egypt the men sit at the loom indoors, while the wives work outside for daily bread. You are the same, my children — those of you who should have borne the burden sit at home like girls, while my daughters labor and drudge in their place, easing their father's misery. The one, ever since she grew from a girl's feebleness into womanhood, has been the old man's guide and shared my weary wandering — often roaming hungry and footsore through wild forest paths, in drenching rains and scorching suns, indifferent to home and comfort, if only her father might have her tender care. And you, my child, once before slipped out past the Cadmeians' watch to bring your father every oracle concerning Oedipus, and made yourself my faithful agent after they banished me. Now what errand brings you from home? What news, Ismene, do you have for your father? This much I know — you have not come empty-handed, without some warning of fresh alarm.

ISMENE. The trouble and toil I took, father, to find where you were living and how you were faring — I spare you. It would be a double pain to live through and then to tell. I come to tell you about the misfortune of your ill-starred sons. At first they were willing to leave the throne to Creon, meaning to clear away the old, ingrained curse — the canker that had infected all your race. But now some god, and their own crazed minds, have stirred up a mad rivalry between them to grab at sovereignty and royal power. Today the hot-headed one, the younger son, is keeping Polyneices from the throne, his elder, and has driven him out of the land. The banished brother, so all Thebes reports, has fled to the vale of Argos. There, through new alliances and friends in arms, he swears he will either establish Argos as lord of the Cadmeian land, or — failing that — raise whoever beats him to the stars of heaven. This is no empty rumor, father, but deadly truth. How long your agony will continue before the gods pity you, I cannot say.
OEDIPUS. Have you really begun to hope that the gods will turn at last and rescue me?
ISMENE. Yes — that is how I read the latest oracles.
OEDIPUS. What oracles? What has been said, child?
ISMENE. They run like this: in time your country will long to have you, living or dead, for their welfare.
OEDIPUS. And who could gain anything from a man like me?
ISMENE. Their sovereignty, it is said, depends on you.
OEDIPUS. So — when I cease to exist, my worth begins.
ISMENE. The gods who once brought you low now raise you up.
OEDIPUS. Poor help, to lift up an old man who fell in his youth.
ISMENE. Be that as it may, it is for this reason alone that Creon is coming to you — and coming soon.
OEDIPUS. With what intent, my daughter? Speak plainly.
ISMENE. To plant you near the Theban land — so they can keep you within their reach, but not let your foot cross the border.
OEDIPUS. What do they gain if I am outside their borders?
OEDIPUS. If the proper burial is refused, your tomb brings a curse on them.
OEDIPUS. It takes no god to tell what is plain to common sense.
ISMENE. That is why they want you close at hand — not where you would be your own master.
OEDIPUS. Do they mean to cover my bones in Theban dust?
ISMENE. No, father — the guilt of a kinsman's blood forbids it.
OEDIPUS. Then they shall never be my masters — never!
ISMENE. Thebes, you will regret this bitterly one day!
OEDIPUS. When does that happen, child? What has to occur?
ISMENE. When they stand at your tomb and feel the anger of your ghost.
OEDIPUS. And who has told you what you are telling me, child?
ISMENE. Envoys who went to consult Delphi.
OEDIPUS. Has Phoebus spoken about me in this way?
ISMENE. So say the envoys who came back to Thebes.
OEDIPUS. And could one of my sons have heard of this?
ISMENE. Yes, both of them — and they know exactly what it means.
OEDIPUS. They knew it — and still the ignoble greed for power outweighed any longing for their father's return.
ISMENE. Your words are bitter — but I have to admit they are true.

OEDIPUS. Then may the gods never quench their deadly feud, and may it be my judgment that decides the fight they are now arming for, spear against spear — so that neither the one who now holds the scepter may keep the throne, nor the one who fled may return. They never raised a hand when I, their father, was thrust from hearth and home. When I was outlawed and banished, what did they care? Will you say it was done at my own request, a favor the state granted because I wished it? Not so. Mark this: on the very day when in the storm of my soul I craved death — even death by stoning — no one stepped forward to carry out that wild longing. But later, when time had dulled my anguish, and I felt that my rage had overrun those old mistakes — that was when the city set itself to drive me out by force, after sparing me for years. And my sons, who as sons should have helped, did nothing. One little word from them was all I needed, and they did not speak a word. They let me wander on forever, a banished man, a beggar. These two girls, their sisters, gave everything their sex could give — food, safe shelter, a daughter's care — while their two brothers sacrificed their father for the lust of power and the scepter of kingship. No — they shall never have me for an ally, and this Theban kingship will bring them no gain. I know this from this girl's oracles, and from those old prophecies about me that Phoebus has now at last brought to pass. Let Creon come, then. Let all the mightiest in Thebes come seeking me. For if you, my friends, championed by those dread local Powers, take up my cause, then you gain for the State a great deliverer, and for my enemies a curse.

chapters.title: First Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. You must stir our pity, Oedipus — you and these girls. And the stronger plea you make — as the savior of our land — inclines me to advise you for your own good.
OEDIPUS. Help me, kind sirs. I will do whatever you tell me.
CHORUS. First, make atonement to the deities whose grove you have trespassed on and profaned.
OEDIPUS. In what way, stranger? Teach me, please.
CHORUS. First, make a libation of water brought with clean hands from a living spring.
OEDIPUS. And once I have this pure water?
CHORUS. You will find bowls, the work of a carver's hand. Wreathe the rims, and wreathe both handles —
OEDIPUS. With olive shoots, or with tufts of wool, or how?
CHORUS. With wool from a freshly sheared yearling fleece.
OEDIPUS. What next? How do I finish the ritual?
CHORUS. Pour out your libation, facing the dawn.
OEDIPUS. Pouring it from the urns you mentioned?
CHORUS. Yes — in three streams. And drain the last bowl to the last drop.
OEDIPUS. And what do I fill it with, before I set it in place? Tell me that too.
CHORUS. With water and honey. Add no wine.
OEDIPUS. And when the shaded earth has drunk it in?
CHORUS. Then with both hands lay on it twenty-seven olive sprays, and offer this prayer.
OEDIPUS. Let me hear it — that is what matters most.

CHORUS. That, since we call them the Gracious Ones, they may grant the suppliant their saving grace. Pray it yourself, or whoever prays for you, in a whisper — not aloud. Then go, and do not look back. Do as I say, and I will stand by you boldly as your friend. Otherwise, stranger, I would have my fears for you.
OEDIPUS. Daughters, do you hear what these strangers say?
ANTIGONE. We heard, father, and we will do as you say.

OEDIPUS. I cannot go, disabled as I am — doubly, by weakness and by blindness. But one of you can do it in my place. One person, I think, can pay the sacrifice for thousands, if the heart is loyal and true. Go do it quickly, but do not leave me alone. This body of mine is too weak to move without a guiding hand.
ISMENE. Then I will go and perform these rites. But where to find the spot — that I still have to learn.
CHORUS. Beyond this grove. If you need anything, the keeper of the precinct will help you.
ISMENE. I am going. You, Antigone, meanwhile must watch over our father. In a parent's cause, trouble — if it is trouble at all — doesn't count.
[Exit ISMENE.]
CHORUS. It is painful, stranger, to wake pain that has long since stopped aching — and yet I would like to hear —
OEDIPUS. Hear what?
CHORUS. The story of your cruel suffering, for which no cure was found — the fate that held you bound.
OEDIPUS. As your guest, I ask this favor — don't make me expose my shame.
CHORUS. The story is told far and wide, and still echoes from one ear to the next. I'd like to hear the truth from you.
OEDIPUS. Oh, oh!
CHORUS. Please give in.
OEDIPUS. Oh, oh!
CHORUS. Grant my request — I granted all of yours.
OEDIPUS. Know then that I suffered the vilest evils — but none, so help me Heaven, came from any act I did with malice.
CHORUS. How so?
OEDIPUS. The State bound a wholly unknowing bridegroom in an impious marriage chain. That was my ruin.
CHORUS. Did you really share an incestuous bed with the woman who gave you birth —
OEDIPUS. It stabs me like a sword, that double-edged word, stranger — but these girls, my own —
CHORUS. Go on.
OEDIPUS. Two daughters — two curses.
CHORUS. O God!
OEDIPUS. Born from the birth-pangs of my own mother-wife.
CHORUS. So your children are at the same time —
OEDIPUS. Too true. Their father's own sisters too.
CHORUS. Oh, the horror!
OEDIPUS. Horrors from the bottomless deep come flooding back over my soul in returning waves.
CHORUS. You have endured —
OEDIPUS. Intolerable agony.
CHORUS. And sinned —
OEDIPUS. I did not sin.
CHORUS. How not?
OEDIPUS. I served the State. I wish I had never won that graceless reward by which I was ruined.
CHORUS. And next, unhappy man — you have shed blood?
OEDIPUS. Must you hear more?
CHORUS. A father's?
OEDIPUS. Flood on flood overwhelms me — that word is a second killing blow.
CHORUS. Murderer!
OEDIPUS. Yes, a murderer — but know this —
CHORUS. What can you plead?
OEDIPUS. A plea of justice.
CHORUS. How so?
OEDIPUS. I killed the man who would have killed me. I killed without intent. A wretched man, yes — but innocent in the eye of the law, I stand without stain.
CHORUS. Look — our sovereign Theseus, son of Aegeus, comes at your summons to do his part.

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: [Enter THESEUS.]

THESEUS. I had often heard of you in the past — the bloody mutilation of your eyes — and so I recognize you, son of Laius. Everything I gathered on the way here made my guess doubly certain. And now your clothes and that ruined face prove it: you are the man. So, pitying your condition, most ill-starred Oedipus, I want to know what you are asking of me and of Athens — you, and the helpless girl at your side. Speak. The tale would have to be grim indeed for me to recoil from it. I too was raised in exile, like you, and wrestled in foreign lands with more dangers than any man. So no stranger in distress will ever seek my help in vain — nor shall you. I know I am mortal, and my share of what tomorrow brings is no greater than yours.

OEDIPUS. Theseus — your words, so fitting, so generous, so comforting, need no long reply. Who I am, what family I sprang from, and from what land I came — you have said it all. So without a preamble I can now make my short request, and my whole story will be told.
THESEUS. Speak. Tell me what I want to know.
OEDIPUS. I come to offer you this worn-out body — a gift not beautiful to look at, yet worth far more than any outward show.
THESEUS. What benefit do you claim to have brought?
OEDIPUS. You will learn that later — not yet, I think.
THESEUS. When can we hope to see the benefit?
OEDIPUS. When I am dead and you have buried me.
THESEUS. You ask for life's last service — and everything before that, is it forgotten, or of no importance?
OEDIPUS. Yes — the last favor guarantees all the rest.
THESEUS. Then the grace you crave is small indeed.
OEDIPUS. No — weigh it well. What is at stake is not trivial.
THESEUS. You mean between your sons and me?
OEDIPUS. Prince, they would like to take me back to Thebes.
THESEUS. If there is no compulsion, then staying in exile doesn't suit you.
OEDIPUS. No — when I wanted to go back, they refused.
THESEUS. For shame! Such a temper is unbecoming in a fallen man.
OEDIPUS. Scold me if you will, but first listen to my plea.
THESEUS. Go on — I want the full story before I judge.
OEDIPUS. Theseus, I have suffered wrong piled on wrong.
THESEUS. Do you mean the old misfortune of your family?
OEDIPUS. No — that has become a byword throughout Greece.
THESEUS. What, then, is this grief that is more than mortal?
OEDIPUS. This is my situation: I was expelled from my country by my own flesh and blood, and I can never return — I am a parricide.
THESEUS. Why would they fetch you home, if you must stay outside?
THESEUS. What does the oracle threaten them with?
OEDIPUS. Destruction waiting for them in this land.
THESEUS. What can breed bad blood between them and me?

OEDIPUS. Dear son of Aegeus, the gods alone are granted immunity from old age and death. Nothing else escapes all-ruining time. The earth's strength decays, the strength of men decays, honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes. There is no constancy between friend and friend, or city and city. Sooner or later, sweet turns to bitter, and hate turns back to love. If now there is sunshine between Thebes and you, and not a cloud, still Time in its endless course gives birth to endless days and nights — and in those days the smallest trifle will be enough for ranks of spears to cut through your bonds of friendship. Then my sleeping, buried corpse in its cold grave will drink up their warm life-blood — if Zeus is still Zeus and Phoebus still speaks true. But enough: it is wrong to tear aside the veil of such mysteries. Let me stop where I began: it is enough if you keep the promise you have sworn. Then you shall never complain that Oedipus was an unprofitable and thankless guest — unless the gods themselves play me false.
CHORUS. The man, my lord, has from the very first declared that he has the power to offer these and similar benefits to our land.

THESEUS. Who could reject the friendship offered by a man like this? First, he can claim the hospitality to which by mutual contract we are pledged. Next, coming here as a suppliant of the gods, he pays full tribute to the State and to me. So I will never spurn his favors. I grant him the full rights of a citizen. And if it suits the stranger to stay here, I place him in your charge. Or if he would rather come with me — choose, Oedipus, which of the two you prefer. Your choice is mine.
OEDIPUS. Zeus — may your blessing fall on men like these!
THESEUS. So what do you decide? Will you come with me?
OEDIPUS. Yes — if it were lawful. But here is rather the place —
THESEUS. What is it you want here? I will not thwart your wish.
OEDIPUS. Here I shall defeat those who cast me out.
THESEUS. Then your presence here would be a great boon.
OEDIPUS. It will prove so — if you keep your pledge.
THESEUS. Have no fear for me. I will not play you false.
OEDIPUS. There is no need to back up your promise with an oath.
THESEUS. An oath would be no more reliable than my word.
OEDIPUS. How will you act, then?
THESEUS. What is it you are afraid of?
OEDIPUS. My enemies will come —
THESEUS. Our friends will see to that.
OEDIPUS. But if you leave me?
THESEUS. Do not teach me my duty.
OEDIPUS. It is fear that makes me press.
THESEUS. My soul knows no fear!
OEDIPUS. You do not know what threats —

THESEUS. I know this — that no one will drag you from here against my will. Such threats, thrown out in anger, are often bluster — idle breath, forgotten when sense returns. And as for your enemies, even if their words are brave and they boast of bringing you back, they are likely to find the seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such is my firm purpose. But in any case, take heart, since Phoebus has sent you here. Even at a distance, my name is enough to protect you from harm.

chapters.title: Second Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. You have come to a horse-famed land for rest, stranger worn out by your journey — to a country that is, of all countries, the loveliest: Colonus with its gleaming soil. It is the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, who hides in her bower among the wine-dark ivy wreathing the vale, and trills her ceaseless song. And she loves the place, where clusters of berries nod over a sunless, windless glade, the spot where no mortal foot has trodden — the pleasure-ground kept for the Bacchic god, where every night he holds his wild revels with the nymphs who raised the lusty child.

And, fed each morning by pearly dew, the starry narcissi shine, and a wreath is twined with the crocus's golden hue for the Mother and the Daughter. The sleepless fountains never cease that feed the stream of Cephisus. They swell the earth's breast with quick new life, and their water has a crystal gleam. The chorus of the Muses will never scorn to visit this heaven-favored plain, nor will the Cyprian queen with her golden reins.

And here there grows, unpruned, untamed, a terror to enemy spears — a tree unknown in Asian soil, unclaimed by the Dorian isle of Pelops, self-renewing year after year: the grey-leaved olive that feeds our children. Neither youth nor withering age destroys the plant — the plant that the Olive Planter tends, and the Grey-eyed Goddess herself protects.

And we boast yet another gift, of all gifts most prized by our fatherland — the might of the horse, the might of the sea. To you, Poseidon, we owe our fame, son of Kronos, our divine king, who first fitted the iron bit for the mouths of horses on these very roads. You also taught us to shape the swift oar-blade for the rower's arm, as swift as the hundred feet of the Nereids as they dance along the sea.
ANTIGONE. O land praised above all lands — now is the time for you to make these glorious titles good.
OEDIPUS. Why this appeal, my daughter?
ANTIGONE. Father — look! Creon is approaching with his company.
OEDIPUS. Have no fear — it shall be so. If we are old, this country's strength has no trace of old age in it.

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: [Enter CREON with attendants.]

CREON. Citizens, my noble friends — you are alarmed at my arrival; I see it in your eyes. Fear nothing, and hold back your angry words. I come with no ill intent. I am old, and I know that the city I am coming to is without equal among the powers of Greece. It was because of my years that I was chosen to persuade your guest to come back to Thebes — not as the delegate of one man, but commissioned by the State, since of all Thebans I, his kinsman, have mourned most bitterly for his sorrows. Listen to me, luckless Oedipus — come home! The whole Cadmeian people rightfully claim to have you back — and I most of all; for more than anyone (else I would be vile indeed), I grieve at your misfortunes, seeing you an aged outcast, wandering on and on, a beggar with only one handmaid to lean on. Ah — who could ever have imagined that she could fall to such a depth of misery, tending in poverty your ruined body, a girl of marriageable age but unmarried, a prey for any wanton ravisher? Does it not seem cruel, this reproach I cast on you and on myself and on all our house? But an open shame cannot be hidden. Hide it — oh hide it, Oedipus — you can. By our fathers' gods, I beg you: consent. Come back to Thebes, come to your father's home, bid Athens a fond farewell as is proper. Thebes, your old foster-mother, has the first claim on you.

OEDIPUS. Brazen-faced man — your subtle tongue would twist every plea of right to your own advantage. Why try your tricks on me? Why set out your snares again in the places where it would hurt me most to be caught? In the old days, when I was distraught from self-inflicted pain and longed for exile as a glad release, your will refused the favor I begged for. But when my frenzied grief had spent itself, and I wanted a taste of home again, then you thrust me from my country. Then these ties of kindred meant nothing to you. And now again — when you see this State and all its kindly people welcoming me — you try to separate us, wrapping hard thoughts in soft words. What pleasure can you possibly find in forcing friendship on unwilling enemies? Suppose a man refused to grant some favor when you kept asking him, and then afterwards, when you had gotten your heart's desire, agreed — granting a kindness from which all kindness had gone — would such a favor not seem an empty gift? That is exactly the gift you are offering me now: fair on the surface, but false when tested. And I will prove you false, so these men can hear: you have come to take me, but not to take me home — to plant me on your borders, so that your State may escape trouble from this land. You shall never get that. What you shall get instead is my ghost to haunt your country forever. And for my sons, this inheritance — no more: just room to die in. Am I not better than you at drawing the horoscope of Thebes? Are my teachers not surer guides than yours — great Phoebus, and the father of Phoebus, Zeus? You are a bought messenger — your tongue is sharper than a sword's edge — and yet your speech will bring you more defeats than victories. Still, I know I am wasting my words. Go, and leave me here. Whatever my lot may be, no one lives badly who lives content.
CREON. Which of us loses more in this exchange — I overthrown by you, or you who overthrow yourself?
OEDIPUS. I will be quite content if your suit fails with these strangers, as it has with me.
CREON. Unhappy man — will the years never make you wise? Must you live on to cast a slur on old age?
OEDIPUS. You have a glib tongue — but I think no honest man can argue well on any side of a case.
CREON. It is one thing to speak much, another to speak well.
OEDIPUS. Your words, of course, are few — and all well aimed!
CREON. Not for a man with wits like yours, no.
OEDIPUS. Go! I order you in the name of these citizens — and do not prowl around me any longer, blockading the harbor that fate has set aside for me.
CREON. I protest to these men, not to you — and as for your answer to your kinsman, if I ever take you —
OEDIPUS. Who, against their will, could take me?
CREON. Even untaken, you shall smart.
OEDIPUS. What power do you have to carry out that threat?
CREON. One of your daughters has already been seized. The other I will carry off in a moment.
OEDIPUS. Oh no, no!
CREON. This is only the beginning of your sorrows.
OEDIPUS. Have you taken my child?
CREON. And will soon have the other.
OEDIPUS. Friends! Surely you will not betray me? Drive this godless villain from your land.
CHORUS. Get out of here, stranger — away with you! You are doing wrong now, and wrong in everything you have done.
CREON (to his guards). It is time to carry off the girl by force, if she refuses to go willingly.
ANTIGONE. Oh, I am lost! Where can I run? Where can I find help, from gods or men?
CHORUS. What do you want, stranger?
CREON. I am not laying hands on him — only on her, who is mine.
OEDIPUS. Princes of this land!
CHORUS. Sir, you are doing wrong.
CREON. No — right.
CHORUS. How right?
CREON. I take only what is mine.
OEDIPUS. Help, Athens!
CHORUS. What is this, man? Let her go, at once — or we fight it out.
CREON. Stand back!
CHORUS. Not until you stop.
CREON. It is war with Thebes if I am touched or harmed.
OEDIPUS. Didn't I warn you?
CHORUS. Quick — let the girl go!
CREON. Order your own servants — I am not your slave.
CHORUS. Stop, I tell you.
CREON (to the guard). Move her!
CHORUS. To the rescue, every one of you! Rally, neighbors, to my call! The enemy is at the gate — rally to defend the State!
ANTIGONE. I am lost! They are dragging me away, friends!
OEDIPUS. Where are you, daughter?
ANTIGONE. Hauled off by force!
OEDIPUS. Your hands, my child!
ANTIGONE. They will not let me reach you, father.
CREON. Take her away!
OEDIPUS. Oh, I am lost — oh, lost!

CREON. So those two crutches will no longer be there to carry you further on your wandering. Since it pleases you to triumph over your country and your friends — whose order I, though a prince, am here carrying out — enjoy your triumph. Sooner or later you will find you are your own worst enemy, now and in the past, when in spite of your friends you gave free rein to the passion that has always been your ruin.
CHORUS. Stop there, stranger!
CREON. Hands off, take care.
CHORUS. Give back the girls, or you do not leave.
CREON. Then Thebes will take a dearer surety soon. I will lay hands on more than these two girls.
CHORUS. What else can you do?
CREON. Carry off this man.
CHORUS. Brave words!
CREON. Deeds will make them good in a moment.
CHORUS. Unless our sovereign intervenes.
OEDIPUS. Shameless voice! Would you lay a hand on me?
CREON. Be silent, I tell you!

OEDIPUS. Goddesses — allow your suppliant to utter one last curse! Wretch — now that my eyes are gone, you have torn away the helpless girl who was my eyes. For this, to you and to all your cursed line, may the great Sun, whose eye sees everywhere, grant length of days and old age like my own.
CREON. Listen, men of Athens — do you mark this?
OEDIPUS. They mark us both, and understand that I, wronged in deed, defend myself with words.
CREON. Nothing will curb my will. Old as I am, and single-handed, I will have this man.
OEDIPUS. Oh, I am lost!
CHORUS. You are a bold man, stranger, if you think you can carry this through.
CREON. I do.
CHORUS. Then I shall no longer think of this as a State at all.
CREON. With a just quarrel, the weak conquer the strong.
OEDIPUS. Do you hear what he says?
CHORUS. Words only — Zeus knows, not yet deeds!
CREON. Zeus may know — but not you.
CHORUS. Insolence!
CREON. Insolence you must put up with.
CHORUS. Hurry, princes — sound the alarm! Men of Athens, to arms! Quickly, to the rescue, before the robbers get their prize home!
[Enter THESEUS.]
THESEUS. Why this outcry? What is going on? Why was I called away from the altar of Poseidon, lord of your Colonus? Speak! On what errand have I come rushing here without a pause?
OEDIPUS. Dear friend — that voice tells me who you are — this man has just now done me a foul wrong.
THESEUS. What wrong, and who has done it? Speak.
OEDIPUS. Creon, who stands before you. He has robbed me of everything — my two daughters.
THESEUS. What does this mean?
OEDIPUS. You have heard the account of what he did.

THESEUS. Quick — one of you, to the altars. Tell my men to leave the sacrifice and hurry, foot and horse, with loose reins, to where the tracks used by packmen split off. Otherwise the two girls will slip away, and I will become a mockery to my guest — a man plundered by force. Quick, as I said. As for this stranger: if I had let my rage, justly stirred up, have its way, he would not have escaped my hands unhurt and uncorrected. But now the very laws he himself appealed to — those, and no others, will judge him. You shall not leave this land until you have fetched the girls and produced them in front of me. You have offended me, and your own race, and your own country. You came to a State that champions right and demands legal warrant for every act, and you set aside the law of the land. Like some freebooter, you carry off whatever plunder pleases you — as if you thought this was a city with no men, or manned by slaves, and as if I were nothing. Yet this villainy was not learned from Thebes. Thebes is not in the habit of breeding unjust sons, and she would not praise you if she knew you were robbing me — and the gods too, by dragging off their suppliants, poor girls. If I were on Theban soil prosecuting the most just claim imaginable, I would never seize my own by violence without the sanction of your State or your king. I would behave as a foreigner should, living among another people. But you shame a city that does not deserve it — your own city — and your long years have made you an old man and a fool. So I tell you again, as before: see that the girls are returned at once — unless you want to stay here by force rather than choice. That much I tell you straight out — and I mean what I say.

chapters.title: Third Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Your case is desperate, stranger. By birth and family you should be a just man — yet you are plainly doing wrong.

CREON. I did not do what I have done thinking this city empty of men or of judgment, son of Aegeus, as you claim. I thought rather that your people would not set such store by kinsmen of mine as to keep them against my will. And I was sure they would not harbor a godless parricide, a reprobate convicted of an incestuous marriage. For on her native hill of Ares here — I knew your far-famed Areopagus — Justice sits, and does not allow vagrants to stay within your borders. Trusting in that, I went hunting for my quarry. Even then I would have held back, but for the dire curses with which he bound my kinsfolk and myself — such a wrong, I thought, gave warrant for what I did. Anger knows no old age; only death can quiet it. The dead alone feel no sting of spite. So work your will. My cause is just, but weak without allies. Yet old as I am, I will try to answer deeds with deeds.

OEDIPUS. Shameless railer — do you think this abuse defames my grey hairs more than your own? Murder and incest — you blurt out these horrors as charges against me, and I have borne them all, no willing sinner. So it pleased the gods, angry perhaps with my sinful race of old, since they could find no sin in me myself for which in retribution I was doomed to trespass this way against myself and mine. Answer me this: if by some oracle my father was destined to a bloody end at a son's hand, how can this reflect on me — on me, then unborn, begotten by no father, conceived in no mother's womb? And if, born to misery, as I was born, I met my father, not knowing who he was or what I was doing, and killed him, how can you justly blame that utterly unconscious hand? As for my mother — wretch, are you not ashamed to force out of me the story of her marriage, since she was your own sister? That marriage I will proclaim at once. I will speak: your lewd and impious words have broken all the bonds of silence. She was, alas, my mother. I did not know it; neither did she. And she, my mother, bore children to the son she herself had borne — a shameful birth. But this much I know: you slander her and me deliberately, while I married without knowing and speak now unwillingly. No — neither in this marriage nor in the deed you keep throwing in my face — a murdered father — shall I be held to blame. Come, answer me one question, if you can: if someone tried right now to take your life, would you — man of justice — first inquire whether the attacker was perhaps your father, or would you turn on him at once? As you love your life, you would turn on your attacker, without stopping to debate, provided the law backed you. Such was my case, and such the position the gods reduced me to. And I think my father, if he could come back to life, would not disagree. Yet you, who are not just but a man who will stop at nothing if it serves his argument, reproach me with this in front of these men. It suits you to praise great Theseus's name and Athens as a wisely governed State. And yet in your flatteries one thing is missing: if any land knows how to render the gods their proper rites, it is Athens most of all. This is the land from which you tried to steal their aged suppliant, and from which you have carried off my daughters. So I turn to those goddesses here, I call on them, I invoke their help to champion my cause — so you may learn what breed of men watches over this State.
CHORUS. An honest man, my lord — one sorely pressed by fortune, and so worthy of our support.
THESEUS. Enough words. The captors are making speed, while we the victims stand here debating.
CREON. What do you want? What can I, a feeble man, do?

THESEUS. Show us the trail, and I will come with you — so that, if the girls are somewhere nearby, you can yourself reveal them to me. But if your guards have outstripped us with their prize, we can rein in. Others are riding ahead, and they will not escape them to thank the gods once safely home. Lead on, I say. The captor is caught; fate has taken the fowler in his own snare. How quickly dishonest gains are lost. And do not look for allies. I know well that such a height of insolence was never reached without backers or accomplices. You have some supporter in this bold venture, but I will probe the matter to the bottom, and see to it that one man does not prevail against the State. Do you take my meaning — or do these words seem as empty as our warnings did when the plot was being hatched?
CREON. Nothing you say can I dispute here — but once at home, I too shall play my part.
THESEUS. Threaten us — and go! You, Oedipus, stay here, certain of this: nothing short of my death will keep me from bringing the girls back.
OEDIPUS. Heaven bless you, Theseus, for your nobleness and all your loving care on my behalf.
[Exeunt THESEUS and CREON.]

CHORUS. Oh, when the fleeing enemy at last turns at bay and begins to trade blow for blow — might I see the fight! Might I hear the loud battle roar swell on the Pythian shore, or by the torch-lit bay where the dread Queen and Maid cherish the mystic rites — rites they betray to no one, before Secrecy's golden key is laid upon the lips by their own acolytes, the priestly Eumolpidae.
There I might see Theseus, our bold captain, meet with the robber band before they have fled the land — and by main force rescue the two captive girls.

Perhaps on the swiftest horse, or in the flying chariot, they are approaching even now the glen west of white Oea's cliff. The raiders will be beaten. Dread are our warriors, dread are Theseus's men. Every bridle flashes bright; every gallant knight charges — all those who adore our Queen, Pallas their patron, or him whose wide flood encircles the earth, the great Ocean-king whom Rhea bore.

Are they fighting, or preparing to fight? A rare vision tells me that soon again I shall see the twin girls, so ill-used, so beaten upon by their own kin. Today, today Zeus is working some great thing. This day shall bring victory. Oh for the wings, the wings of a dove — to be carried on the gale's speed, up and still upwards, and gaze on the fight from the clouds above! All-seeing Zeus, lord of heaven — grant our guardian host triumphant might, to surprise the fleeing foe and take back their prize. Hear us, Zeus, and hear us, child of Zeus — Athene undefiled. Hear, Apollo, hunter — hear, Huntress, sister of Apollo, who chase the dappled, swift-footed deer over the wooded glade. Help Athens in this hour of danger with your twofold power! Traveler — you will not have to charge the friends who watch for you with a false prophecy. Look — an escort with the girls is drawing near.

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS.]
OEDIPUS. Where? Where? What are you saying?
ANTIGONE. Father, father — if only some god would grant you eyes to see this best of men, who brings us back to you.
OEDIPUS. My child! You are really back?
ANTIGONE. Yes — saved by Theseus and his gallant men.
OEDIPUS. Come to your father's arms. Let me feel the embrace of a child — a thing I never hoped for again.
ANTIGONE. What you ask is doubly sweet to give.
OEDIPUS. Where are you, then?
ANTIGONE. We come to you together.
OEDIPUS. My precious nurslings!
ANTIGONE. Fathers have always been tender.
OEDIPUS. Props of my old age!
ANTIGONE. Sorrow propped up by sorrow.

OEDIPUS. I have my darlings. If death should come now, death would not be wholly bitter, with you near me. Cling to me — press close on either side — rest here from your dreary wanderings. Now tell me what you went through, but keep it short. Brief speech suits young girls like you.
ANTIGONE. Here is our savior. You should hear the story from his own lips. Then my part will be brief.

OEDIPUS. Do not be surprised, I beg you, if the sight of children I had given up for lost has drawn my talk out a little too long. I know very well that the joy I have in them is due to you, to you and to no one else. You alone delivered them — no one else. May the gods deal with you according to my prayer — with you and with this land! For I have found here, more than anywhere on earth, reverence for heaven, uprightness, and lips that do not lie. I say this in gratitude for what I know. Everything I have, I owe to you alone. Give me your hand, prince, that I may touch it — and if you will allow me, let me kiss your cheek. But what am I saying? How can I wish you to touch a man as fallen as I am — a man reduced to utter wretchedness, corrupted and stained with a thousand evils? No — I would not let you, even if you wished. Only those who have known calamity themselves can share in it. Let me greet you from where I stand. And continue to befriend me as you have done until now.

THESEUS. I do not wonder that you lingered in talk with your children, and preferred their conversation to mine. I feel no jealousy. I prefer to be famous by deeds rather than words. Of this, old friend, you have had proof. I have kept my oath and brought the girls back alive and unharmed, for all his threats. How the fight was won I will not waste words boasting — your daughters themselves will tell you everything. But there is a matter that came up recently on my way here, on which I would like your counsel — a small thing, it seems, but worth some thought. A wise man pays attention to everything, great or small.
OEDIPUS. What is it, son of Aegeus? Let me hear. About what you ask, I know nothing.
THESEUS. They say that a man — no countryman of yours, but one of your kin — has taken sanctuary beside the altar of Poseidon, where I was making sacrifice when I was called away.
OEDIPUS. What is his country? What does the suppliant ask?
THESEUS. I know only one thing — that he begs, they tell me, for a word with you. He will not trouble you.
OEDIPUS. What is he asking? If a suppliant, it must be serious.
THESEUS. They say he is only waiting to speak with you, and then to go unharmed on his way.
OEDIPUS. I wonder who this petitioner can be.
THESEUS. Think whether there is anyone among your kin at Argos who might claim such a favor from you.
OEDIPUS. Dear friend — stop, I beg you.
THESEUS. What is the matter?
OEDIPUS. Do not ask it of me.
THESEUS. Ask what? Explain.
OEDIPUS. Your words have already told me who the suppliant is.
THESEUS. Who can he be, that I should frown on him?
OEDIPUS. My son, king — my hated son, whose voice of all men's would grate most on my ears.
THESEUS. Surely you can at least listen to him. If his request offends, you need not grant it. Why so reluctant even to hear him?
OEDIPUS. That voice grates on a father's ears, king. I have come to loathe it. Do not force me to give way.
THESEUS. But he has taken sanctuary. Beware — do not fail in due reverence to the god.

ANTIGONE. Listen to me, father — young as I am. Let the prince have his way, and do what in his eyes is service to the god. For our sake also — let our brother come. If what he asks is not for your good, he cannot force your will. What harm in hearing him? A plot of villainy is soon exposed by open words. You are his father; so you cannot repay a son's most impious outrages in kind. Listen to him. Other men like you have thankless children and quick tempers, but by yielding to the gentle spell of persuasion they let their savage mood be charmed away. Look to the past, forget the present; think of all the grief your father and mother brought you. From that you will draw this lesson without fail — that evil passion ends in evil. You have, alas, stern reminders to prick your memory — these forever sightless eyes. Give in to us. Just petitioners should not have to beg over and over, and one who accepts a favor should have the grace to return it.
OEDIPUS. The favor you win by pleading, my child, is bitter to me. Still — have it your way. Only this, my friend: if he must come, I beg you, let no one have the power to take me away.
THESEUS. No need, sir, to ask a second time. I don't like to boast — but be assured, your life is safe as long as any god keeps mine safe.
[Exit THESEUS.]

CHORUS. Whoever longs for length of days, scorning the common span of life — I judge him a giddy fool, walking in the ways of folly. For the long years heap up a heavy load — pleasures few, pains heavier — until not one joy remains for the man who lingers on life's weary road. And come it slow or fast, one doom of fate awaits us all alike — for the dance and the marriage bell, for the dirge and the funeral knell. Death the deliverer sets all free at last. Not to be born at all — that is best, the best thing that can happen. Next best, once born, is to go back the way you came, with the least delay. For when youth passes with its giddy company, trouble follows trouble, toil follows toil — pain, pain forever pain — and no one escapes life's coils. Envy, sedition, strife, carnage and war — these make up the sum of life. And last comes the worst and most despised stage — forgotten old age, joyless, friendless, slow — the crowning evil of all evils.

Such ills not I alone have known — our guest here has known them too. Like some headland on an iron-bound shore, lashed by winter winds and the roar of the surge, he is battered on every side by the overwhelming tide of misfortune — beaten by every wind of heaven, some from the sunset, some from the dawn in the east, some from the glow of noon, some from the Rhipean gloom of everlasting snow.
ANTIGONE. Father, I think I see the stranger coming — alone, and weeping many tears.
OEDIPUS. Who can it be?
ANTIGONE. The same one we guessed from the start — Polyneices. He is here.
[Enter POLYNEICES.]

POLYNEICES. Oh — sisters, shall I first lament my own troubles, or my old father's, whom I find here a castaway with you in a foreign land, an old beggar dressed in grotesque rags that mar his whole figure, while over his sightless eyes his unkempt hair floats in the wind — and, as if to match, he carries a bag against the pinch of hunger? All this I learn too late, wretch that I am. I own it — I stand proved the most vile in neglect of you. I despise myself. But since Zeus in all he does has Mercy enthroned beside him as his partner, father, let Mercy sit enthroned also in your heart. Past wrongs can be amended — they cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Speak, father — do not turn away. Have you no word? Will you dismiss me in mute contempt, without even telling me what you are angry about? You, his daughters, my sisters — try to move this sullen, stubborn silence. Do not let him spurn me — a suppliant of the god — without a single word of reply.
ANTIGONE. Tell him yourself, unhappy man, what your errand is. Many words may send a thrill of joy, or stir a chord of anger or tenderness — and somehow give even the tongue-tied a tongue.

POLYNEICES. You advise me well, and I will speak out. First I call on the god himself as my aid — Poseidon, from whose altar I was raised, with warrant from the monarch of this land, to speak with you and depart unharmed. These pledges, strangers, I ask you and my sisters and my father to observe. Now, father, let me tell you why I came. I have been banished from my native land because, by right of being the elder born, I claimed possession of your sovereign throne — from which Eteocles, my younger brother, ousted me. Not by weight of precedent, nor by the ultimate arbitration of war, but by winning over the people. The prime cause of this, I believe, is the curse resting on you. So also say the seers. And so, when I came to Argos in the Dorian land and married the daughter of King Adrastus, I enlisted under my standard all the foremost captains of the Apian isle, to muster with their help the sevenfold army of spearmen against Thebes — resolved either to throw out my enemies or die in a just cause. Why then, you ask, am I here today? Father, I come as a suppliant to you — for myself and for my allies, who now with seven squadrons under their seven spears surround the whole plain circling Thebes. First comes the peerless warrior and peerless seer, Amphiaraus, with his lightning spear. Next an Aetolian, Tydeus, son of Oeneus. Third, Eteoclus of Argive birth. The fourth is Hippomedon, sent to war by his father Talaos. Fifth, Capaneus, who boasts that he will fire and raze the town. Sixth, Parthenopaeus, an Arcadian, named after the maid long a maid and late-wed, Atalanta, whose true-born son he is. And last, I, your son — or yours at least in name, though the bastard of an evil fate — leading the fearless Argive army against Thebes. So by your children and your life, father, we all beg you to let go of your anger, and to favor one who seeks just revenge against a brother who has banished and robbed him. For victory, if the oracles speak true, will fall to those who have you for ally. So, by our springs and our household gods, I pray you — yield, and hear me. I am a beggar and an exile, you an exile likewise. We are both caught in the same misfortune, and we find a home as pensioners — while he, the lord of Thebes, makes a mockery of both of us. That agony! With a breath I will scatter the upstart's power. I will bring you back home and establish you there — and, having thrown him out, establish myself. With your goodwill I will undertake all this. Without it, I can scarcely come back alive.
CHORUS. For the sake of the king who sent him, Oedipus, do not dismiss him without a fitting reply.

OEDIPUS. No, worthy elders — but for Theseus's sake, who sent him here to have word with me, he would never have heard my voice again. Now he shall receive this parting favor — an answer that will bring him little joy. Villain — when you held the sovereignty that your brother now holds in your place, did you not drive me, your own father, out? Make me an exile, cityless, and make me wear this beggar's clothing you weep to see, now that you have come yourself to my sad plight? There is nothing here for tears. I must bear it until death. And I shall think of you as my murderer. You thrust me out. It is you who have made me intimate with misery — through you I beg my bread in a strange land. If these daughters of mine had not tended me, I would have been dead for any help from you. They tend me, they keep me alive, they are men and not women in their true service to their father. But you are bastards — no sons of mine. So just Heaven has an eye on you — though not yet with the stern face you will soon know, if indeed these banded armies are moving on Thebes. You can never take that city. First you shall fall, you and your brother, both stained with each other's blood. Such was the curse I launched on you two some time ago, and such is the curse I now call on to fight for me — so that you may learn to honor those who gave you birth, and not to mock a blind father who fathered degenerate sons. These girls did not mock me. Therefore my curse is stronger than your 'throne' and your 'suppliance,' if by right of eternal laws primeval Justice sits enthroned with Zeus. Be gone — loathed, disowned, no son of mine, vilest of the vile! And take with you this curse I leave you as my last bequest: never to win your native land by arms, no, nor to return to Argos in the Vale — but to die by a kinsman's hand, and to kill the man who expelled you. So I pray, and I call on the ancestral gloom of Tartarus to snatch you from here; I call on these dread goddesses; I call on Ares, who kindled this deadly enmity between you. Go now, and proclaim to all the Cadmeians, your staunch allies, what you have heard — this is the inheritance that Oedipus divides between his sons.
CHORUS. Your errand, Polyneices, did not please me from the beginning. Now go back, and quickly.

POLYNEICES. Woe to my journey, and to my thwarted hopes! Woe to my comrades! What a desperate end to that glad march from Argos! I cannot even whisper this to my allies, or turn them back. I must go mute to meet my doom. My sisters — you, his daughters — you have heard our stern father's prayers. If his curse should come to pass, and you some day return to Thebes, do not disown me, I beg you. Grant me burial and the due funeral rites. Then the praise your daughterly care now wins for you will be doubled by the service you render for me.
ANTIGONE. One favor, Polyneices — let me ask it.
POLYNEICES. What is it, sweet Antigone? Speak.
ANTIGONE. Turn your army back to Argos with all speed. Do not ruin yourself and Thebes along with you.
POLYNEICES. That cannot be. How could I lead an army again if they had seen their leader flinch?
ANTIGONE. But, brother — why stir up anger again? What gain from the ruin of your country?
POLYNEICES. Living in exile is a disgrace. Shall I, the elder, put up with a younger brother's taunts?
ANTIGONE. Then will you bring to pass his prophecies — the one who threatens you both with mutual slaughter?
POLYNEICES. Yes — that is what he wishes. But I must not give way.
ANTIGONE. Oh, I am undone! But tell me — who will dare, having heard his prophecy, to follow you?
POLYNEICES. I will not tell it to them. A good general reports successes and conceals setbacks.
ANTIGONE. Misguided boy — your resolve stands firm, then?

POLYNEICES. It does — and do not try to stop me. The road I choose, hounded by my father and his avenging spirit, leads me to ruin. But for you — may Zeus make your path bright, if you carry out what I ask when I am dead. In life, you cannot help me further. Now let me go — farewell, a long farewell. You will never see my living face again.
ANTIGONE. Oh no!
POLYNEICES. Do not lament me.
ANTIGONE. Who would not mourn you, brother — rushing into an open grave?
POLYNEICES. If I must die, I must.
ANTIGONE. No — hear my plea.
POLYNEICES. It cannot be. Stop.
ANTIGONE. Then I am desolate — if I must lose you.
POLYNEICES. That rests with fate — whether I live or die. But for the two of you, I pray to heaven that you may escape all harm. You are blameless in everyone's eyes.
[Exit POLYNEICES.]

chapters.title: Fourth Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Evils upon evils — no pause, no rest! Do they come from our sightless guest? Or are we seeing fulfilled at last what fate has long willed? For never yet have I found anything vain that the heavenly powers ordain. Time, with ever-wakeful eye, watches what is written on high — now overthrowing the great, now raising the lowly. Listen! How the thunder rumbles! Zeus defend us!
OEDIPUS. Children, my children — will no messenger go and summon Theseus here, my best friend?
ANTIGONE. Why do you summon him, father?
OEDIPUS. This winged thunder of the god is about to carry me to Hades. Send for him — do not delay.

CHORUS. Listen — with louder, nearer roar the bolt of Zeus descends again. My spirit quails and cowers. My hair stands on end with fear. Another flash! What does the lightning portend? Always it points to grave outcomes. Dread powers of the air! Save — Zeus, save us!
OEDIPUS. Daughters — the appointed end has come for me. There is no turning from it now.
ANTIGONE. How do you know? What sign has convinced you?
OEDIPUS. I know it well. Let someone go with all speed and summon the Athenian prince.

CHORUS. Listen — once more the deafening sound peals louder all around. If you darken our land, lay your hand on it lightly, lightly. Grace, not anger, let me win — if on a man of sin I have looked with a pitying eye. Zeus our king, I cry to you!
OEDIPUS. Is the prince coming? When he comes, will he find me still living, and my senses clear?
ANTIGONE. What solemn charge do you want to lay on him?
OEDIPUS. For all his kindnesses, I would keep the promise I made when I first received them.

CHORUS. Hurry here, my son — rise, leave the altar and the sacrifice, if you are paying your vow to Poseidon in the far glade. Our guest would bring you and your people a proper offering, a due reward. Hurry, King!

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: [Enter THESEUS.]

THESEUS. Why this general clamor again? My people are calling me, and the stranger is calling me. Is it a thunderbolt from Zeus, or a sleet of arrowy hail? A storm as fierce as this would justify any fear of disaster.
OEDIPUS. Prince — you come just when you are most wanted. Some god must have sent good luck along with you on the way.
THESEUS. What has happened now, son of Laius?
OEDIPUS. My life is tipping in the scale. I want to do everything I promised you and your people before I die.
THESEUS. What sign tells you that your end is near?
OEDIPUS. The gods themselves are the heralds of my fate. None of their appointed warnings fails.
THESEUS. How do they signify their will, you say?
OEDIPUS. This thunder, peal on peal — this lightning, flash on flash — hurled from the unconquered hand.
THESEUS. I must believe you, having often found you a true prophet. Speak then — what must be done?

OEDIPUS. Son of Aegeus — I will unfold for this state a treasure that time cannot corrupt. Myself, without anyone to guide me, I will presently take you to the spot where I must end. Never reveal this secret to any mortal — neither the spot nor where it lies. So it shall serve you as a defense, better than native shields and near allies. But those dread mysteries that speech may not profane, you yourself shall gather when you come there alone. I cannot reveal them to any of your subjects, nor even to my own children, though I love them dearly. You must guard them alone, and whisper them to your chosen heir alone, so that they may be passed on from heir to heir. Thus you shall hold this land inviolate against the dread Dragon's brood. The most just State may still be wronged by countless reckless neighbors — for the gods, though they delay, still mark for doom the godless sinner in his mad career. Far from you, son of Aegeus, be any such fate. But now — the god within me urges me on. To the spot, and no more hesitation. Follow me, daughters, this way. Strange that I, whom you have led so long, should lead you now. Oh, do not touch me. Let me find on my own the grave that destiny has set for me in this land. Here — this way — for Hermes the guide leads this way, and Persephassa, queen of the dead. O light — no light to me, but mine before — now for the last time I feel you palpably, for I am nearing the final gloom of Hades. Blessing on you, dearest friend — on you and on your land and your followers. Live prosperous, and in your happy state, think still, for your own welfare, of me, the dead.
[Exit THESEUS, followed by ANTIGONE and ISMENE.]

CHORUS. If the prayers of mortals are heard in hell — hear us, dread, invisible goddess! Monarch of the dreary regions, Aidoneus, hear, oh hear! By a gentle, tearless doom, speed this stranger on his way to the gloom. Let him enter without pain the all-shrouding Stygian plain. Wrongfully oppressed in life, let him now be blessed by Justice.

Queen of the underworld — and you, fierce watchdog of the gates of hell, who, as legend says, glare and snarl in your cavernous lair at all who come — let him go unharmed to the fields below. For your master orders it so — the son of Earth and Tartarus. Keep the monster in its den, giver of eternal sleep.
[Enter MESSENGER.]
MESSENGER. Friends, countrymen — my news, in sum, is that Oedipus is gone. But the event was not brief, and the story cannot be briefly told.
CHORUS. What — has he gone, the unhappy man?
MESSENGER. Know this for certain: he has passed from life to death.
CHORUS. How? By a god-sent, painless doom, poor soul?

MESSENGER. Your question points to the marvel of the tale. How he moved from this place — you saw it, and know it — without a friend to lead the way, himself guiding all of us. When we had reached the abrupt Earth-rooted Threshold with its bronze stairs, he paused at one of the converging paths, close to the rocky basin that records the pact of Theseus and Peirithous. Between that cleft and the Thorician rock, the hollow pear-tree and the marble tomb, midway he sat down and stripped off his beggar's clothing. Then he called to his daughters and told them to fetch running water, both for washing and for libation. They climbed the slope, and soon brought back what their father had asked for. Then they bathed and dressed him with the proper rites. When he had his way in everything, and no desire was left unsatisfied, there came a thunder from the underworld. The girls shivered, crouched at their father's knees, wept, beat their breasts and broke into a long lament. He, hearing their sudden bitter cry, folded his arms around both of them and said: 'My children — you will lose your father today. All of me has perished, and you will no longer have to bear the long, long service you have given. A heavy burden, I know — and yet one word wipes out all the tally of troubles: love. And you had love from me — as much as from any man alive. But now you must live all your days without me.' So, clinging to each other, father and daughters both sobbed and wept. But when at last their mourning had an end, and no cry went up, there was a moment of silence. Suddenly a voice summoned him. Every hair stood on end in sudden fear, and all of us were stunned. For the call came now loud, now low, and over and over: 'Oedipus, Oedipus — why do we linger? Too long, too long your passing is delayed.' When he heard the summons of the god, he asked that Theseus be brought; and when the prince drew near, 'O my friend,' he cried, 'pledge my daughters, giving your right hand — and, daughters, give him yours — and promise me that you will never forsake them, but do all that time and friendship prompt for their good.' And he, of his nobility, held back his tears and swore to be their constant friend. With that promise given, Oedipus stretched out his blind hands, laid them on his children, and said, 'My children — prove your true nobility now. Go away from here, and do not seek to see sights that are forbidden, or to hear forbidden words. Go, quickly. Let no one stay but Theseus, our ruler, to see what happens next.' So we all heard him speak. And weeping bitterly, we accompanied the girls on their way. A little later, we looked back — and he was gone, vanished from our sight. Only the king we saw, shading his eyes with his hand, as if from some awful vision that no man could bear to look upon. A moment later, we saw him bend in prayer — to Earth, and to Heaven, at once. But by what doom the stranger met his end, no one knows except Theseus. No fiery bolt struck him down in that hour, no whirlwind came off the sea — he was simply taken. It was a messenger from heaven, or else some gentle, painless opening of the earth. For without lament, without sickness, without pain, he passed away — the most marvelous end. And if my tale seems foolish to some, I am content to be called a fool by such men.
CHORUS. Where are the girls and the friends attending them?
MESSENGER. They cannot be far off. The sound of lamentation coming closer tells that they are on their way here.
[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE.]

ANTIGONE. Oh, oh — on this bitter day we two sisters of a blighted line must bow beneath the blow. We must weep, and weep again, the curse that lay on our father — for whom in life a lifelong world of care was ours to bear, and in death we must face the gloom that wraps his tomb. What tongue can tell that unspeakable sight?
CHORUS. What are you saying, girls?
ANTIGONE. It is all only guessing.
CHORUS. Is he gone, then?

ANTIGONE. Gone — in the very way you would most wish for him. Not in battle or in a storm at sea, but taken from sight, carried by unseen hands to the unseen fields of night. I am undone. On us too a night has come down — the night of mourning. Where shall we wander, over land or sea in our misery, eating the bread of bitterness?
ISMENE. I do not know. Oh, that Death might nip my breath, and let me share my old father's fate. I cannot live a life as desolate as this.
CHORUS. Best of daughters, worthy pair — what heaven brings you, you must bear. Fret no more against Heaven's will. Fate has not dealt with you badly.

ANTIGONE. Love can turn past pain to joy. What seemed bitter is now sweet. That happy labor is sweet to me — the guidance of those dear blind feet. Dear father, forever wrapped in the gloom below, even in the grave you shall never lack love — her love and mine.
CHORUS. His end —
ANTIGONE. Was exactly as he planned.
CHORUS. How so?

ANTIGONE. He died, as he wished, in a foreign land. Wrapped in kindly earth, he sleeps his long last sleep, and his friends weep over his grave. How great our loss is, these streaming eyes can tell. Nothing can quell this sorrow. You had your wish — to die this way among strangers. But I — alas — not at your side.
ISMENE. Alas, my sister — what new fate
[Text lost in manuscript.]
[Text lost in manuscript.]
comes upon us, desolate orphans?
CHORUS. His end was blessed. So, children, check your grief. Man is born as fate's prey.
ANTIGONE. Sister, let us go back again.
ISMENE. Why go back?
ANTIGONE. My soul longs —
ISMENE. Longs?
ANTIGONE. To see the earthy bed.
ISMENE. You mean?
ANTIGONE. Where our father lies.
ISMENE. No — you cannot. Do you not see —
ANTIGONE. Sister, why are you angry with me?
ISMENE. Don't you know — besides —
ANTIGONE. Must I hear more?
ISMENE. He died without a tomb, with no one near him.
ANTIGONE. Lead me there — kill me there.
ISMENE. How am I, unhappy, to go on — friendless, helpless — how to drag out a life of misery alone?
CHORUS. Do not be afraid, girls —
ANTIGONE. Ah — where shall we run?
CHORUS. Refuge has been found.
ANTIGONE. For me?
CHORUS. Where you shall be safe from harm.
ANTIGONE. I know.
CHORUS. Why then this alarm?
ANTIGONE. How we are to get home again — I do not know.
CHORUS. Why then wander?
ANTIGONE. Troubles overwhelm us —
CHORUS. As before.
ANTIGONE. Worse than what was worst before.
CHORUS. Truly you are driven on the surge of the breakers.
ANTIGONE. Alas — we are.
CHORUS. Alas — it is so.
ANTIGONE. Where shall we turn, Zeus? No ray of hope to light the way along which the fates are driving our desperate journey.
[Enter THESEUS.]
THESEUS. Dry your tears. When grace is shed on the living and on the dead by the dark, kindly Powers, they resent excessive grief.
ANTIGONE. Son of Aegeus, to you we pray.
THESEUS. What is the favor, children? Speak.
ANTIGONE. With our own eyes we want to see our father's tomb.
THESEUS. That cannot be.
ANTIGONE. What are you saying, King?

THESEUS. My children, he charged me strictly that no mortal should approach the sacred threshold, or greet with funeral laments the hidden grave where he lies. He said: 'If you keep my command, you shall hold your realm in peace.' The God of Oaths heard this promise, and to Zeus I pledged my word.

ANTIGONE. Well — if that is what he wanted, we must yield. Then let us go back to Thebes, if we still can, to heal this deadly feud and stop the self-inflicted doom that drives our brothers to the grave.
THESEUS. Go in peace. I will spare no effort and no devoted care, but will attend to all your needs — gladdening my friend in his grave.
CHORUS. Wail no more. Let sorrow rest. All is ordered for the best.
